summary.text: The decolonisation of Africa was a series of political developments from the mid-1950s to 1976, during the Cold War, as colonial governments gave way to sovereign states.
Colonial rule came from the Scramble for Africa, when European powers claimed almost all of the continent between 1870 and 1914, and its end often involved violence and organised revolts.
By 1977, 50 African countries had gained independence from European colonial powers.

items.prompt: European powers confirmed the partition of Africa at a conference in 1885, ignoring existing political and social structures. What happened to Africa's precolonial states?

options.label: Most kept their sovereignty under European protection
Almost all lost their sovereignty, with Liberia and Ethiopia the exceptions
Most merged into one African federation
Most became allies of the colonisers on equal terms

items.explain: Almost all precolonial states lost their sovereignty; only Liberia and the Ethiopian Empire were exceptions.

items.prompt: An African soldier returns home after serving a colonial power in World War II. What was a likely result of that service?

options.label: Deeper political awareness and expectations of more self-determination
A guarantee of equal treatment from the colonial regime
Public praise from colonial powers for his contribution
A prompt withdrawal of colonial powers from his homeland

items.explain: Service led to deeper political awareness and expectations of respect and self-determination, which went largely unfulfilled; colonial powers downplayed Africans' contributions.

items.prompt: Roosevelt and Churchill issued a charter about people choosing their own government. Churchill said it covered only nations of Europe under Nazi rule, while Roosevelt thought it applied worldwide. How did anticolonial politicians read it?

options.label: As covering only the nations of Europe
As a binding treaty approved by both legislatures
As having no bearing on their own situation
As relevant to colonial empires right away

items.explain: Anticolonial politicians immediately saw the Atlantic Charter as relevant to colonial empires, even though it was not a ratified treaty.

items.prompt: A mining company in a colony sends its profits to shareholders in Europe while local development is neglected. What did this cause?

options.label: Rapid growth of local industry paid for by those profits
Wider local support for colonial government
Significant local socioeconomic grievances
Calls for more European shareholders to invest

items.explain: Diverting profits to European shareholders at the expense of internal development caused significant local socioeconomic grievances.

items.prompt: In the 1930s, colonial powers helped educate a small elite of local African leaders at Western universities. What did those leaders become familiar with there?

options.label: Ideas such as self-determination
Methods for keeping colonial rule permanent
The plans for dividing Africa among European powers
Orders to enlist in European armies

items.explain: At Western universities these leaders became familiar with ideas such as self-determination.

items.prompt: A 1960 international declaration said colonial exploitation denies human rights. What did it say should happen to power?

options.label: It should stay with colonial powers until they chose to leave
It should be transferred back to the countries or territories concerned
It should pass to the United Nations to run directly
It should be shared equally with the colonial powers

items.explain: The UN declaration stated that power should be transferred back to the countries or territories concerned.

paragraphs.heading: Colonies become nations
paragraphs.text: The decolonisation of Africa was the series of political changes, from the mid-1950s to 1976, in which colonial governments fell and sovereign states took their place. It happened during the Cold War and swept across the continent, often with violence, unrest and organised revolts. Its major events included the Algerian War, the Mau Mau rebellion, the Congo Crisis, the Zanzibar Revolution and Angola's War of Independence. By 1977, 50 African countries had won independence from European colonial powers.

paragraphs.heading: How the colonies began
paragraphs.text: Those colonial governments dated from the Scramble for Africa, from 1870 to 1914, when European powers raced to claim nearly the whole continent and its natural resources while avoiding war among themselves. The Berlin Conference of 1885 confirmed the division, paying no attention to the political and social structures already there. Almost every precolonial African state lost its sovereignty; the exceptions were Liberia and the Ethiopian Empire, though Italy occupied Ethiopia in 1936. Britain and France held the most, but Germany, Spain, Italy, Belgium and Portugal had colonies too.

paragraphs.heading: Africans in the world wars
paragraphs.text: Many Africans served in both world wars. In the First, African labour was vital on the Western Front, yet many Africans were barred from carrying weapons or serving as equals with whites. In the Second, Africans fought in Europe and Asia, and about a million from sub-Saharan Africa served in European armies in some role; many were forced to enlist, while some volunteered for better prospects than civilian work offered. The experience deepened political awareness and raised hopes of respect and self-determination that mostly went unmet. Because the Allies meant to keep their colonies and lean on them to rebuild Europe, they played down what Africans had done for victory.

paragraphs.heading: A charter and new ideas
paragraphs.text: In 1941 Roosevelt and Churchill met to plan the post-war world, and the result was the Atlantic Charter. Its third clause spoke of people's right to choose their form of government and of restoring self-government. Churchill told Parliament it meant the nations of Europe under Nazi rule, but Roosevelt saw it as applying everywhere, and anti-colonial politicians at once saw its meaning for empires. In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights stated that everyone is born free and equal. Earlier, in the 1930s, a small group of Africans educated at Western universities had met ideas such as self-determination there.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure from within
paragraphs.text: At home, grievances built up. Colonial economies sent profits from mining and other resource extraction to European shareholders instead of local development, causing serious social and economic resentment. During the Second World War, when U-boats in the Atlantic disrupted the shipping of raw materials to Europe, some African industries and towns grew. Over time towns, industries and trade unions expanded, literacy and education improved, and pro-independence newspapers appeared. In 1945 the Fifth Pan-African Congress demanded an end to colonialism, with future presidents of Ghana, Kenya and Malawi among its delegates.

paragraphs.heading: Independence arrives
paragraphs.text: After the war, independence spread fast across Africa. Italy lost its African empire, including Libya, Eritrea, Somalia and Ethiopia, as a result of World War II. Colonies such as Nigeria, Senegal and Ghana pressed for self-government while the colonial powers were worn out by war. In 1960 a United Nations declaration said colonial exploitation denies human rights and that power should pass back to the countries or territories concerned.
